set.detail:
On 28 March 193 some 300 Praetorians, angered by Pertinax's discipline and his failure to pay the full donative, marched into the palace and killed him after only 87 days. With no obvious successor, the Guard shut itself in the Castra Praetoria. Inside, Pertinax's father-in-law Titus Flavius Sulpicianus, prefect of the city, began bargaining for the throne; outside the wall the wealthy senator Marcus Didius Julianus, a former governor of Germania Inferior and Africa, shouted counter-offers, reportedly holding up his fingers to show the sums. Cassius Dio, a senator in Rome at the time, says Sulpicianus had reached 20,000 sesterces per man when Julianus jumped to 25,000 (6,250 denarii) and warned the soldiers that Sulpicianus would avenge Pertinax. The gates opened, and the Guard escorted Julianus to the Senate under arms; the senators, Dio among them, ratified the choice out of fear.

The 'auction' became the classic image of imperial decadence, but its importance lay in what followed. The plebs jeered Julianus at the Circus, occupied it for a day and night and called on Pescennius Niger in Syria to save them. Within weeks three provincial armies had proclaimed their commanders: Severus on the Danube (9 April), Niger in Syria and, in effect, Clodius Albinus in Britain. Julianus tried to fortify the city, train elephants and marines, send assassins against Severus, and finally offered him a share of power. The Praetorians, softened by years in Rome, were useless, and the Senate deserted him once Severus reached Italy. On 1 June 193 the Senate condemned Julianus to death, and a soldier killed him in the palace; Dio reports his last words as 'What evil have I done? Whom have I killed?' He had reigned 66 days.

Herodian's version is more rhetorical and the Historia Augusta, more sympathetic, claims Julianus was pushed into the bid by his family. Modern historians (Birley, Hekster) stress that the episode exposed the Guard as a political liability and opened the door to a civil war decided by the frontier armies, ending the Antonine model of senatorial consensus.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Birley, Septimius Severus: The African Emperor (2nd ed., 1988)

set.detail:
Lucius Septimius Severus, born at Lepcis Magna on 11 April 145 into a Punic-Italian family of equestrian and senatorial rank, had governed Gallia Lugdunensis and Sicily and in 191 was appointed legate of Pannonia Superior, with three legions at Carnuntum, Vindobona and Brigetio. His brother Geta governed Moesia Inferior, and friends held other Danube commands, so that when news of Pertinax's murder arrived the whole Danube army, sixteen legions from the Rhine to the Black Sea, could be swung behind him. On 9 April 193 the troops at Carnuntum hailed him Augustus; he took the name Pertinax and presented himself as avenger of the murdered emperor rather than as a rival of Julianus.

Severus acted with remarkable speed. To secure his rear he offered Clodius Albinus, governor of Britain with three legions, the rank of Caesar and implied succession, which Albinus accepted. He then marched on Italy with a picked force, covering some 800 miles in about two months; Ravenna and its fleet were taken, the Julian Alps were left undefended, and Julianus' envoys and assassins either failed or changed sides. Severus ordered the Praetorians to hand over Pertinax's killers, which they did. On 1 June the Senate deposed Julianus, and Severus entered Rome in early June, staying about a month before marching east against Pescennius Niger, who had been proclaimed by the Syrian legions at about the same time.

Dio, who knew Severus, records dreams and omens that the emperor himself publicised in his autobiography, including a vision of being carried on a horse to the Forum. Herodian contrasts Severus' cunning with the slowness of Niger. The proclamation inaugurated a dynasty that lasted, with the interruption of Macrinus, until 235 and reoriented the empire around the army, the African and Syrian connections of Severus and his wife Julia Domna, and a much more openly military monarchy.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Birley, Septimius Severus: The African Emperor (1988)

set.detail:
After Julianus' death the Senate sent a delegation of a hundred senators to meet Severus at Interamna, where they were searched for daggers before admission. Before entering Rome Severus ordered the Praetorians to parade outside the city unarmed, in ceremonial dress, as if to swear the oath. Surrounded by his Illyrian legionaries, they were harangued for the murder of Pertinax and the sale of the empire, stripped of their military belts, daggers and insignia, and dismissed in disgrace, with orders not to come within a hundred miles of Rome on pain of death. Their horses were taken; Dio reports that one horse followed its rider and both were killed.

Severus then entered the city on foot in civilian dress, though his army followed in arms and camped in temples and porticoes, a scene Dio, an eyewitness, describes as the most brilliant he had seen and yet alarming. Severus swore before the Senate that he would put no senator to death without trial, an oath he soon broke. A new Guard was formed, ten cohorts probably of a thousand men each (perhaps 1,500), recruited not from Italy, Spain, Macedonia and Noricum as before but from the best soldiers of all the legions, overwhelmingly Danubians. Severus also enlarged the urban cohorts and vigiles and later stationed II Parthica at Albanum.

Dio complained that the change filled Rome with uncouth soldiers terrifying to hear and see, and drove the young men of Italy into banditry or gladiatorial schools, since a career in the Guard was closed to them. Modern scholarship (Campbell, Speidel) sees the reform as a turning point: the Guard became a corps of elite legionaries and a military reserve that fought in the Parthian and British wars, and the legions gained a channel of promotion into Rome. It survived until Constantine abolished it after the Milvian Bridge in 312.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Campbell, The Emperor and the Roman Army (1984)

set.detail:
The rupture between Severus and Albinus came after Severus, having defeated Niger, declared his elder son Caracalla Caesar in 195-196, effectively disinheriting Albinus, who then took the title Augustus and crossed to Gaul with the British legions. Albinus based himself at Lugdunum and defeated Severus' general Virius Lupus; a mint at Lugdunum struck his coins. Severus came west through Pannonia and Noricum, and after a preliminary victory at Tinurtium (Tournus) on the Saône the decisive battle was fought near Lugdunum on 19 February 197.

Dio, whose figure of 150,000 men on each side is certainly inflated, describes a long and evenly matched struggle. Albinus' left wing was routed and fled to its camp, but on the right his men dug concealed pits and trenches in front of their line, lured the Severan troops forward with a feigned retreat and inflicted heavy losses. Severus brought up the Praetorians, was nearly killed, lost his horse and in one version tore off his imperial cloak and drew his sword to rally the fugitives. The cavalry under Julius Laetus then arrived and decided the day; Dio claims Laetus had deliberately held back to see which side would win, and Severus later executed him. Albinus fled to a house by the Rhône and killed himself or was killed; his head was sent to Rome, and Severus rode his horse over the naked body before it was thrown into the river with those of his wife and sons.

Lugdunum, capital of the Three Gauls, was sacked and burned and never fully regained its pre-eminence, while Trier rose. In Rome Severus read to the Senate a eulogy of the severity of Sulla, Marius and Augustus and executed 29 senators, and confiscations of the property of Albinus' partisans in Gaul and Spain enriched the res privata. Herodian and the Historia Augusta offer different details; the exact site, perhaps on the plateau north of the city around Trévoux, remains unknown.
set.debate: Size of the armies (Dio: 150,000 each) and exact site disputed; role of Laetus contested.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

set.detail:
While Severus was fighting Albinus, the Parthian king Vologaeses V attacked Roman Mesopotamia and besieged Nisibis. Severus returned east in the summer of 197, relieved Nisibis and, at the Euphrates, built a river fleet. The army sailed and marched downstream past Dura, found Seleucia and Babylon abandoned, and reached Ctesiphon, the Parthian winter capital on the Tigris, which was stormed in late 197 or January 198. Vologaeses escaped with a few horsemen, but the city was given over to plunder; Dio says the soldiers killed all the adult males and took about 100,000 captives, along with the royal treasure.

On 28 January 198, the hundredth anniversary of Trajan's accession, Severus took the title Parthicus Maximus, raised the ten-year-old Caracalla to Augustus and made Geta Caesar, a choreographed link with Trajan, the last emperor to take Ctesiphon. The army, short of supplies, then withdrew up the Tigris, the Euphrates route having been stripped of forage, and Severus twice failed to take the desert city of Hatra in 198 and 199, the second time, Dio says, because he called off an assault that had breached the walls in the hope of saving the temple treasures, by which time his European troops refused to attack again.

The campaign is commemorated on the Arch of Septimius Severus in the Forum (203), whose four large panels depict the sieges of Nisibis, Edessa or Carrhae, Seleucia and Ctesiphon in the style of campaign paintings. Its long-term significance was greater than its immediate gains: the humiliation of the Arsacid house, the third Roman sack of Ctesiphon in eighty years, contributed to the internal discredit that allowed Ardashir to overthrow the dynasty in 224. Dio judged the annexations that followed costly and provocative, a view many modern historians share.
set.debate: Date of the capture (late 197 or January 198) disputed.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

set.detail:
Severus owed his throne to the army and is remembered, by Dio and Herodian alike, for binding it to the dynasty with money and privileges. Legionary pay, unchanged since Domitian at 300 denarii a year, was raised, probably to 400 or 450 denarii (Caracalla raised it again by half, perhaps to 675); donatives grew, and a regular allowance in kind (later the annona militaris) became a burden on the provinces. Herodian says Severus allowed soldiers to live with their wives, effectively lifting the Augustan ban on marriage for serving men, legalising families that already existed around the forts. He also granted soldiers the right to wear the gold ring of the equestrian order, opened promotion from the centurionate into equestrian posts, and ordered the collegia of principales and junior officers formed at Lambaesis and elsewhere.

Three new legions, I, II and III Parthica, were raised for the eastern war and commanded by equestrian prefects rather than senatorial legates, a pattern that pointed towards Gallienus' later exclusion of senators. I and III Parthica garrisoned the new province of Mesopotamia at Singara and Rhesaina, while II Parthica was stationed at Albanum near Rome. With the doubled Praetorian Guard, the enlarged urban cohorts and vigiles, and the equites singulares, the emperor kept roughly 30,000 troops at the capital.

Dio quotes Severus' dying advice to his sons to 'enrich the soldiers and scorn all others', and Gibbon called him the principal author of the decline of the empire. Modern scholars are more cautious. Brian Campbell and Michael Speidel point out that pay had lost value through inflation and that the reforms professionalised rather than barbarised the army; the debate concerns how heavily the rising wage bill drove the debasement of the denarius and later the antoninianus, and whether Severus' openness to promotion from the ranks created the soldier-emperors of the following decades.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Speidel, "Roman Army Pay Scales", JRS 82 (1992)
Campbell, The Emperor and the Roman Army (1984)

set.detail:
Roman Mesopotamia began with Severus' first eastern campaign of 195, when he punished Osroene, Adiabene and Arab allies of Niger and restored Roman control over the territory between the Euphrates and the Khabur. After the sack of Ctesiphon and the failures at Hatra, the land was organised as a province under an equestrian prefect on the Egyptian model, so that no senator could command its legions. I Parthica was based at Singara and III Parthica at Rhesaina, and Nisibis, the key fortress city controlling the road from the Tigris to the Euphrates, became the colonia Septimia Nisibis and seat of the governor. The client kingdom of Osroene, ruled from Edessa by Abgar VIII 'the Great', who had visited Rome, was reduced to a small territory around the city; Caracalla deposed its dynasty and made Edessa a colonia in 213-214.

Cassius Dio, who opposed the annexation, wrote that Severus claimed it as a bulwark for Syria, but that it was a constant source of wars and expense, since it lay near the Medes and Parthians and Rome was always fighting for those who lived there. Modern historians have often agreed that the forward position committed Rome to a frontier on the Khabur and the Jebel Sinjar that a revived Persia could not accept. Nisibis and Carrhae changed hands repeatedly in the third century (lost c. 235-238, regained by Timesitheus in 243, lost and regained in the 250s and 260s), and in the fourth Nisibis held off Shapur II three times (338, 346, 350) before Jovian surrendered it in 363.

The province thus defined the Roman-Persian frontier for 165 years and was the scene of the most important sieges of late antiquity. Inscriptions and the Dura parchments show prefects, legionary vexillations and a dense network of forts linking the Euphrates and Tigris.

scholarship: Millar, The Roman Near East 31 BC-AD 337 (1993)
Edwell, Between Rome and Persia (2008)

set.detail:
In 207 the governor of Britain reported that the Caledonii and Maeatae were overrunning the province and asked for troops or the emperor himself. Severus, now over sixty and crippled by gout, came in 208 with Julia Domna, both sons and much of the court. Herodian adds the motive of removing his quarrelling sons from the luxuries of Rome. Eboracum became the seat of government, and Geta was left to administer the province while Severus and Caracalla advanced north in 209, building roads through forests and causeways across marshes. A new legionary base at Carpow on the Tay and the refurbished harbour at South Shields and the fort at Cramond supported the campaign, which may have reached the Moray Firth.

The Caledonians avoided pitched battle, using ambush, bogs and lures of cattle, and Dio claims, implausibly, that the Romans lost 50,000 men. Severus nevertheless forced a treaty by which the enemy ceded territory, and in 210 he and his sons took the title Britannicus. When the Maeatae and Caledonii rose again, Severus ordered a war of extermination, quoting Agamemnon in Homer that no one should escape, not even the child in its mother's womb; Caracalla led the 210 campaign because his father was ill. The Hadrian's Wall system was heavily rebuilt in these years, so that medieval and early modern writers credited Severus with building the Wall itself.

Severus died at York on 4 February 211. Caracalla immediately made peace, withdrew from the newly occupied territory and returned with Geta to Rome, abandoning Carpow. The Severan settlement nonetheless brought nearly a century of relative peace to the northern frontier, perhaps through treaties and subsidies with the northern peoples, and the division of Britain into two provinces followed. Scholars debate whether Severus aimed at the conquest of the whole island or a punitive war followed by a strengthened frontier.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Birley, The Roman Government of Britain (2005)
Hodgson, Hadrian's Wall (2017)

set.detail:
Severus died at Eboracum on 4 February 211, aged 65, after nearly eighteen years of rule. Gout had disabled him for years, and the Caledonian campaign of 210 had to be led by Caracalla. Dio reports that Caracalla had tried to kill his father on horseback in front of the army during a parley with the Caledonians and that Severus, though aware, had pardoned him; Herodian says Caracalla tried to persuade the doctors to hasten his death. The dying emperor's words to his sons, as reported by Dio, were 'Be harmonious, enrich the soldiers and scorn all others'; his last watchword to the tribune was 'Laboremus' ('Let us work'). He is also said to have remarked, 'I took over a state in turmoil everywhere and leave it at peace even in Britain'.

His body was cremated at York, apparently in the presence of the army, and his ashes taken by his sons in an urn of purple stone, or gold, to the Mausoleum of Hadrian. He was promptly deified. The succession passed jointly to Caracalla, Augustus since 198, and Geta, Augustus since 209/210, an arrangement that collapsed within ten months in fratricide.

Severus' reign transformed the monarchy. He fought three civil wars, doubled the troops near Rome, raised the army's pay and status, created Mesopotamia, divided large provinces to prevent rebellion, and favoured equestrians and jurists such as Papinian, Ulpian and Paul in the administration. He lavished buildings on Rome and his native Lepcis. Gibbon blamed him for the military despotism of the following century; modern biographers such as Anthony Birley present an able, ruthless provincial who completed the integration of Africa and the east into the governing class, while acknowledging that the costs of his army policy weighed on his successors.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Birley, Septimius Severus: The African Emperor (1988)

set.detail:
Caracalla (born 188) and Geta (born 7 March 189) had hated each other since childhood, competing in quail-fighting and chariot racing, and their father's attempt to bind them by naming both Augustus failed. After returning from Britain they lived in the imperial palace in Rome with the connecting passages walled up and separate guards; each feared poisoning. Herodian reports a plan to divide the empire, with Geta taking the east from Asia, ruling from Antioch or Alexandria, and Caracalla Europe and Africa, the Senate and armies split along the Propontis, until Julia Domna asked how they proposed to divide their mother.

In late December 211, under the pretext of a reconciliation meeting arranged by their mother in her apartments, Caracalla had centurions burst in and stab Geta, who died in Julia Domna's arms; she was wounded in the hand by his blood-soaked attackers and was forbidden to mourn. Caracalla rushed to the Praetorian camp, claimed he had escaped a plot, and secured the soldiers with a donative of 2,500 denarii each and a pay rise of fifty per cent. The legion at Albanum at first shut its gates, saying it had sworn to both sons.

A purge followed in which, Dio says, 20,000 people died, including Geta's freedmen and soldiers, the jurist and prefect Papinian, Pertinax's son, and Cornificia, daughter of Marcus Aurelius. Geta suffered damnatio memoriae on an unparalleled scale: his name was chiselled from inscriptions across the empire, his portraits defaced, his face scraped from the Severan family tondo now in Berlin and his figure removed from the Arch of the Argentarii in Rome; papyri show his name deleted in Egypt. The date is usually given as 26 December 211, though some scholars prefer 19 December or early 212. The murder poisoned Caracalla's reign and made him, in the hostile tradition, the archetypal tyrant.
set.debate: Date (19 or 26 December 211, or early 212) and the historicity of the partition plan disputed.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

set.detail:
The Constitutio Antoniniana, issued by Caracalla probably in 212 (some argue 213 or 214), granted Roman citizenship to all free inhabitants of the empire except, apparently, the dediticii. It ended the distinction between citizens and peregrines that had structured Roman society since the Republic. Our knowledge depends on a brief notice in Cassius Dio, a sentence of Ulpian in the Digest ('those who are in the Roman world have been made Roman citizens by a constitution of the emperor Antoninus') and a damaged Greek papyrus in Giessen (P.Giss. 40, col. I), which presents the grant as a thank-offering to the gods for the emperor's preservation, probably from Geta's alleged plot.

Dio, hostile to Caracalla, claimed the real motive was fiscal: new citizens became liable to the 5 per cent inheritance and manumission taxes, which Caracalla doubled to 10 per cent, payable to the military treasury. Others stress ideology: Caracalla's universalism, the religious language of the papyrus, and the culmination of a long process of enfranchisement. The meaning of the excluded dediticii is the most debated question: surrendered barbarians, Egyptian villagers, freedmen of the lowest category, or a narrow technical group.

The effects were visible at once in nomenclature. Millions of new citizens took the emperor's family name, so that 'Marcus Aurelius' became the most common name in the eastern papyri. Roman law spread, at least in principle, to all, though local law persisted in practice. The legal line of privilege shifted from citizen versus foreigner to the honestiores versus humiliores, the latter liable to torture and degrading penalties. Later writers such as Augustine and Justinian attributed the measure to Antoninus Pius, showing how its author had faded from memory. Recent studies (Lavan, Ando, Buraselis) emphasise that it extended a Roman identity across the empire just as the third-century crisis began.
set.debate: Date (212 vs 213/214), motive (fiscal, religious, ideological) and the meaning of the dediticii are debated.

scholarship: Sherwin-White, The Roman Citizenship (2nd ed., 1973)
Ando (ed.), Citizenship and Empire in Europe 200-1900: The Antonine Constitution after 1800 Years (2016)
Buraselis, Theia Dorea (1989)

set.detail:
In 215, while preparing his Parthian war, Caracalla introduced a new silver coin, called by modern numismatists the antoninianus after a phrase in the Historia Augusta. It is identified by the radiate crown worn by the emperor, while empresses appear on a crescent moon, signs that it was a double denomination. Weighing about 5.1 grams against the contemporary denarius of about 3.2 grams, and of similar silver fineness, around 50 per cent, it contained the silver of about 1.5 denarii while presumably being tariffed at two, a disguised devaluation that let the treasury stretch its bullion to pay the army whose wages Caracalla had just raised by half.

Macrinus and Elagabalus continued it briefly, but it was dropped around 219, and Severus Alexander struck none, perhaps because it was distrusted. It was revived in 238 by Balbinus and Pupienus and under Gordian III became the main silver coin, driving the denarius out of production by the 240s. From then on its weight and fineness fell rapidly: by the reign of Gallienus and in the issues of Claudius II and the Gallic emperors of the late 260s the silver content had fallen to around 2-3 per cent and sometimes below, the coins being little more than bronze with a silver wash. Hoards of thousands of these 'radiates' from the period 260-274 are among the commonest finds in Britain and Gaul, including barbarous imitations.

Aurelian's reform of 274 restored a heavier radiate with a fixed 5 per cent silver content marked XXI, and Diocletian replaced the system in 294. The antoninianus is thus the clearest physical index of the third-century fiscal crisis. Debate continues about its official name (argenteus antoninianus, radiatus or simply argenteus) and its exact value, which has been inferred mainly from weights and from the parallel double sestertius.

scholarship: Walker, The Metrology of the Roman Silver Coinage III (1978)
Harl, Coinage in the Roman Economy, 300 BC to AD 700 (1996)

set.detail:
Caracalla wintered at Edessa in 216-217 after his first invasion of Parthia, during which, according to Herodian, he had tricked Artabanus IV with a marriage proposal and massacred Parthian nobles at a wedding feast, though Dio says only that Artabanus refused the match. On 8 April 217, travelling with a small escort from Edessa to the temple of the Moon god Sin at Carrhae, he dismounted to relieve himself and was stabbed by Julius Martialis, an evocatus who resented being refused promotion to centurion (Herodian adds that his brother had been executed). Martialis was killed at once by a Scythian archer of the bodyguard. Caracalla was 29 and had reigned six years since his father's death.

The plot was organised by the praetorian prefect Marcus Opellius Macrinus, a Mauretanian equestrian lawyer, who had learned that letters from Rome were warning the emperor that an astrologer had predicted Macrinus would reign; since Macrinus handled the emperor's correspondence, he intercepted one and acted before he could be denounced. Two tribunes of the Guard, the Aurelii Nemesianus and Apollinaris, were involved. For three days the army had no emperor; on 11 April the soldiers proclaimed Macrinus, who professed grief, had Caracalla's ashes sent to Julia Domna at Antioch and allowed his deification to placate the troops, who idolised the dead emperor.

Macrinus was the first emperor who was not a senator. He had to fight Artabanus at Nisibis, bought peace for 200 million sesterces, and tried to cut the soldiers' pay rises, which proved fatal: in May 218 the Syrian legions declared for Caracalla's supposed son Elagabalus, promoted by Julia Maesa. Julia Domna, ill with breast cancer and fearful of being reduced to private status, starved herself to death at Antioch. Dio, then in Pergamum as Macrinus' appointee, is the main and well-informed source.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

set.detail:
Ardashir, son (or adopted son) of Papak and grandson of Sasan, priest of the temple of Anahid at Istakhr, began as a local ruler in Persis and in the 210s-220s conquered the neighbouring kingdoms of Kerman, Isfahan and Mesene, exploiting the Parthian civil war between Artabanus IV and his brother Vologaeses VI. When Artabanus finally marched against him, the armies met on the plain of Hormozgan, whose location is unknown, perhaps near Ram Hormoz in Khuzestan. Arabic and Persian tradition (Tabari, drawing on the Sasanian Book of Kings) dates the battle to 28 April 224 and says Ardashir killed Artabanus with his own hands, while his son Shapur killed the Parthian secretary Dadbundad. The great rock relief at Firuzabad shows three equestrian duels: Ardashir unhorsing Artabanus, Shapur his opponent and a page another Parthian noble.

Ardashir spent two more years subduing Media and the rest of the Parthian realm and was crowned King of Kings of Eran at Ctesiphon, probably in 226. He took the title 'King of Kings of the Iranians whose lineage is from the gods' and founded cities such as Ardashir-Khwarrah (Firuzabad) and Veh-Ardashir opposite Ctesiphon. Branches of the Arsacid family survived in Armenia, which became a long-term point of conflict.

For Rome the change was momentous. Dio, writing in 229, already warned that Ardashir was a fearful threat; Herodian states that he claimed all lands once held by the Achaemenids up to the Aegean, though modern scholars such as Kettenhofen and Potter doubt whether such irredentism was real Sasanian policy or Roman projection. In any case the new dynasty was more centralised, militarily aggressive and ideologically Zoroastrian, and within twenty years its kings had raided Mesopotamia, killed one Roman emperor (Gordian III) and would soon capture another.
set.debate: Date (224 or 227) and location of the battle; reality of Sasanian Achaemenid claims.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Wiesehöfer, Ancient Persia (1996)
Daryaee, Sasanian Persia (2009)

set.detail:
After an indecisive Persian campaign in 232, Severus Alexander and his mother Julia Mamaea were called west by Germanic attacks on the Rhine and Danube. In 234 he assembled an army at Mogontiacum, including eastern archers and Osrhoene troops, and built a pontoon bridge across the Rhine. Instead of fighting, however, he opened negotiations and offered money for peace, a policy the soldiers saw as cowardly and as diverting to barbarians funds that should have been theirs. Mamaea's dominance and reputed avarice deepened the resentment.

In March 235 recruits from Pannonia, being trained by the gigantic Thracian equestrian officer Gaius Julius Verus Maximinus, proclaimed their commander emperor. When the news reached the imperial camp at Vicus Britannicus (probably Bretzenheim near Mainz), Alexander's own troops deserted; he was found clinging to his mother in his tent, and both were killed together with their advisers. He was 26 and had reigned thirteen years. Herodian, the only contemporary narrative, describes the scene; the Historia Augusta places it in Britain or Gaul, confusingly. Alexander was later deified, and a tradition associates the Monte del Grano tomb outside Rome, where the Portland Vase was reputedly found, with him and his mother.

The murder ended the Severan dynasty and is conventionally taken as the start of the so-called crisis of the third century, the half-century of short-lived soldier emperors that followed. Maximinus, the first emperor to rise from the ranks and never to visit Rome, symbolised the new dominance of the Danubian army. Modern historians debate how far Alexander's reign really was the peaceful, Senate-friendly regime portrayed by the Historia Augusta, which idealises him, and stress the strain of fighting on two frontiers at once that Herodian's narrative reveals.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Potter, The Roman Empire at Bay AD 180-395 (2nd ed., 2014)

set.detail:
The 'crisis of the third century' is a modern label, popularised in German scholarship (Reichskrise) and by Rostovtzeff and Alföldy, for the half-century between the murder of Severus Alexander (235) and the accession of Diocletian (284). In those 49 years some 26 emperors were recognised in Rome, almost all of them killed by their own troops or in battle, alongside dozens of regional usurpers. At the worst moment, after Valerian's capture in 260, the empire split into three: the Gallic Empire in the west (260-274), the Palmyrene sphere in the east, and Gallienus' central rump.

The pressures were simultaneous. In the east the new Sasanian dynasty killed or captured two emperors (Gordian III at Misiche, Valerian at Edessa) and sacked Antioch. On the Danube Gothic, Carpic and Herul invasions culminated in the death of Decius at Abritus (251) and the seaborne raids that burned Ephesus and Athens; on the Rhine the Franks and Alamanni broke through, and the Agri Decumates were lost around 260. A great pandemic, the Plague of Cyprian, raged from about 249 to the 260s. The silver content of the antoninianus fell from about 50 per cent to under 5, and prices in Egypt rose many times over, especially after Aurelian's reform. Cities in Gaul built tight walled circuits; Rome itself was given walls in 271. The habit of setting up inscriptions collapsed, which partly explains the poverty of our evidence: no contemporary narrative survives beyond fragments of Dexippus, and later sources (Zosimus, Zonaras, the Latin epitomes and the unreliable Historia Augusta) are thin.

Recovery came from Gallienus' reforms (mobile cavalry, equestrian commanders), the Illyrian soldier emperors Claudius II, Aurelian and Probus, and above all Diocletian's restructuring. Historians now debate the very concept. Christian Witschel and others stress regional variation: Africa and parts of the east prospered, and urban life continued in many places. Kyle Harper adds climate change and pandemic as drivers; MacMullen and Potter emphasise the government's responses. Most still see a real systemic crisis, but one that produced the transformed late Roman state rather than collapse.

scholarship: Alföldy, Die Krise des Römischen Reiches (1989)
Witschel, Krise, Rezession, Stagnation? (1999)
Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017)
Hekster, Rome and Its Empire, AD 193-284 (2008)

set.detail:
Maximinus' fiscal pressure fell heavily on the rich of the provinces. In early 238 a procurator in Africa Proconsularis pressed landowners around Thysdrus (El Djem) with demands for arrears; young men of the local aristocracy armed their rural workers, killed him at a meeting and went to the proconsul, Marcus Antonius Gordianus Sempronianus Romanus, a wealthy senator of about eighty from an old family, and proclaimed him emperor. He accepted, reluctantly according to Herodian, and took his son Gordian II, his legate, as co-Augustus. They moved to Carthage and wrote to Rome, where the Senate, delighted, recognised them, declared Maximinus a public enemy, killed his supporters including the prefect of the city, and appointed a board of twenty consulars (vigintiviri) to defend Italy. Provinces across the empire followed.

The revolt was crushed within about three weeks. Capelianus, governor of Numidia and a personal enemy of the elder Gordian, marched on Carthage with legio III Augusta and Moorish auxiliaries. Gordian II led out a large but untrained militia and was killed in battle; his father hanged himself with his belt. The chronology is much disputed: Herodian implies a reign of 22 days, the Historia Augusta 36, and modern reconstructions place it anywhere from January to April 238.

The consequences went far beyond Africa. Having broken with Maximinus, the Senate could not turn back, and elected two of the vigintiviri, Pupienus and Balbinus, as emperors, adding the boy Gordian III, grandson of Gordian I, as Caesar to satisfy the urban mob. Maximinus' invasion stalled before Aquileia, where his soldiers killed him; the Praetorians then murdered Pupienus and Balbinus, leaving Gordian III. Legio III Augusta was disbanded in punishment. The great amphitheatre of Thysdrus, one of the largest in the empire, dates roughly from this period and was never completely finished.
set.debate: Chronology of 238 (length of the Gordians' reign; dates of Aquileia) intensely debated (Peachin, Drinkwater).

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

set.detail:
In 243 Gordian III's army, directed by his father-in-law Timesitheus, drove the Persians out of Roman Mesopotamia, defeating Shapur near Rhesaina and recovering Carrhae and Nisibis. After Timesitheus died of illness, his successor as prefect, the Arabian equestrian Marcus Julius Philippus, advanced with the young emperor down the Euphrates towards Ctesiphon. Early in 244 the armies met at Misiche (Mesiche, probably near modern Fallujah) where, according to the trilingual inscription of Shapur I at Naqsh-e Rostam (ŠKZ), 'Gordian Caesar raised a force from the whole Roman empire, from the Goths and Germans, and marched on Assyria against Eranshahr and against us. On the border of Assyria at Misiche a great frontal battle took place. Gordian Caesar was killed and the Roman force destroyed. And the Romans made Philip Caesar.' Shapur renamed the town Peroz-Shapur, 'Victorious is Shapur'.

Roman sources tell a different story. They never admit a defeat. Zosimus and the Historia Augusta say Philip engineered a supply shortage, stirred the soldiers against the 19-year-old emperor and had him killed; others say he died of illness or a fall from his horse. The soldiers built him a cenotaph at Zaitha near Circesium, which Ammianus saw in 363. Some scholars think Gordian died of wounds from the battle, as the Persian relief at Bishapur implies by showing him lying under Shapur's horse.

Philip, proclaimed emperor, quickly made peace: according to the ŠKZ he paid 500,000 denarii as ransom and became tributary, and he apparently abandoned support for Armenia, though he kept Mesopotamia. He then hurried to Rome. The episode illustrates the difficulty of writing third-century history: the Persian royal propaganda and the Roman literary tradition must be read against each other (Kettenhofen; Dodgeon and Lieu).
set.debate: Whether Gordian died in or after the battle, by wounds, illness or murder by Philip.

set.detail:
The pandemic known after Bishop Cyprian of Carthage broke out, according to later chroniclers, in Ethiopia and reached Egypt around 249, spreading westward to Italy and Africa by 251-252 and recurring in waves for perhaps fifteen to twenty years. Cyprian's sermon De Mortalitate (c. 252) describes diarrhoea that drained the body's strength, fever in the marrow causing sores in the throat, constant vomiting, bloodshot eyes, gangrene of the feet and other extremities, and loss of hearing or sight among survivors. Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria wrote that the city's population had fallen so far that the number of people aged 14 to 80 receiving the grain dole now equalled those formerly aged 40 to 70. The Historia Augusta claims 5,000 deaths a day at Rome.

The disease killed the emperor Hostilian in 251 and was blamed for the death of Claudius II in 270; it disrupted recruitment and armies, contributed to the perception that the gods were angry (one motive suggested for the Decian and Valerian edicts) and depopulated cities and countryside. At Thebes in Egypt Italian excavators found a mass burial in the funerary complex of Harwa and Akhimenru, with bodies covered in lime and kilns for producing it, dated to the mid-third century and linked to this plague.

The pathogen is unknown. Smallpox, measles, influenza and, recently, a viral haemorrhagic fever such as a filovirus (Kyle Harper) have been proposed; no ancient DNA has yet been recovered. Christian writers stressed the contrast between pagans who abandoned the sick and Christians who nursed them; Pontius says Cyprian organised care for all, and Rodney Stark argued that such care raised Christian survival rates and boosted conversion. The plague's demographic and fiscal effects are central to modern arguments that disease, as much as war, drove the crisis of the third century.

scholarship: Harper, "Pandemics and Passages to Late Antiquity", JRA 28 (2015)
Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017)
Tiradritti, "Of Kilns and Corpses", Egyptian Archaeology 44 (2014)

set.detail:
Soon after his accession late in 249, Decius ordered all inhabitants of the empire to sacrifice to the gods, pour a libation and taste the sacrificial meat in the presence of local commissioners, by a set deadline, and to receive a signed certificate. Some 46 such libelli survive on papyrus from Egypt, dated June to July 250, including one for a priestess of the crocodile god Petesouchos, which show that the measure applied to everyone, not only Christians. James Rives has interpreted the edict as an attempt to create a unified religion of empire, a collective act of piety to secure the gods' favour at the millennium's turn and in a time of war and plague, rather than a targeted persecution. For Christians, however, the effect was the first empire-wide test.

The bishop of Rome, Fabian, was executed on 20 January 250, Babylas of Antioch and Alexander of Jerusalem died in prison, and Origen was tortured at Caesarea. Pionius of Smyrna was burned on 12 March 250; Dionysius of Alexandria escaped arrest by accident; Cyprian of Carthage went into hiding and governed his church by letter, which later cost him authority. Large numbers complied: the sacrificati who sacrificed, the thurificati who offered incense, the libellatici who bribed officials for certificates. Others, the confessors, endured prison and torture, and claimed the right to forgive the lapsed.

The persecution faded after Decius' death at Abritus in June 251, but its aftermath split the church. Rigorists rallied around Novatian in Rome and laxists around Felicissimus in Carthage, while Cornelius and Cyprian forged a middle way through councils that imposed graded penance. The number of executions was probably modest, but the experience of mass apostasy shaped ecclesiology, the sacrament of penance and, ultimately, the Donatist controversy of the next century.

scholarship: Rives, "The Decree of Decius and the Religion of Empire", JRS 89 (1999)
Clarke, The Letters of St. Cyprian I-IV (1984-89)

set.detail:
In 250 a great Gothic coalition under King Cniva crossed the Danube. One force besieged Novae and was driven off by Trebonianus Gallus, governor of Moesia; Cniva moved to Nicopolis, where Decius defeated him, then crossed the Haemus. At Beroe (Augusta Traiana) the Goths surprised and routed Decius' army, and they went on to take Philippopolis, where the governor Lucius Priscus proclaimed himself emperor with Gothic support; the city was sacked and Ammianus later claims 100,000 died. In the spring of 251 Decius, with his son Herennius Etruscus, now Augustus, tried to cut off the Goths as they withdrew north with their booty and captives.

The armies met near Abritus (modern Razgrad in north-east Bulgaria) in June 251. According to Jordanes, drawing on Dexippus, Cniva drew up his men in three lines, the third concealed behind a marsh. Herennius was killed early by an arrow; Decius declared that the loss of one soldier mattered little and pressed on. The Romans broke the first two lines but, pursuing into the swamp, were trapped in the mud and annihilated by missiles. Decius' body was never found. Zosimus and Zonaras accuse Gallus, who commanded part of the army and became emperor, of treacherously advising the attack across the marsh, a charge modern historians treat with caution.

Decius was the first Roman emperor killed by a foreign enemy in battle, and the shock was profound: Christian writers such as Lactantius saw it as divine punishment for the persecution. Gallus made a humiliating treaty allowing the Goths to leave with their prisoners and promising annual payments. Hoards buried around Abritus and coin finds in the area testify to the disaster, and excavations at Hisarlaka near Razgrad have explored the later fortress of Abritus.
set.debate: Exact site and the role of Trebonianus Gallus.

scholarship: Bursche, "The Battle of Abritus, the Imperial Treasury and Aurei in Barbaricum", NC 173 (2013)

set.detail:
Shapur I's second great campaign against Rome is known mainly from his own trilingual inscription at the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht (ŠKZ). After the treaty with Philip in 244, Shapur says, 'Caesar lied again and did wrong to Armenia', probably by supporting the Armenian Arsacids against Persia; Armenian tradition remembers the murder of King Khosrov, instigated by Persia, and the flight of his son Tiridates to the Romans. Shapur first invaded Armenia, then turned on Roman Syria. 'At Barbalissos we annihilated a Roman force of 60,000', the inscription continues, 'and Syria and the surroundings of Syria we burned, ruined and pillaged'. It then lists 37 cities captured in this campaign, from Anatha on the Euphrates to Antioch, Hierapolis, Beroea, Chalcis, Apamea, Raphanaea, Zeugma, Cyrrhus, Seleucia, Samosata and others in Syria, Commagene and Cappadocia.

Barbalissos (Balis, near Meskene) lay on the right bank of the Euphrates where the river turns east, a natural invasion route from Mesopotamia into northern Syria. The Roman sources say nothing about the battle, and the figure of 60,000 is a round number of royal propaganda; but the subsequent capture of Antioch shows that the Roman field army in Syria had been destroyed. The emperor Trebonianus Gallus was occupied with the Goths and the plague, and only the local initiative of Uranius Antoninus at Emesa checked the invaders.

The date is debated: most scholars place it in 252 or 253, connected with the sack of Antioch in 253, though some prefer 256 for parts of the campaign. Either way it inaugurated the most catastrophic decade in Rome's eastern history, ending with Valerian's capture in 260. The episode is a reminder that much third-century history must be reconstructed from Persian royal inscriptions, Syriac and Armenian traditions and archaeology rather than Greco-Roman narratives.

scholarship: Dodgeon and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars AD 226-363 (1991)
Kettenhofen, Die römisch-persischen Kriege des 3. Jahrhunderts n. Chr. (1982)

set.detail:
Antioch on the Orontes, with perhaps 200,000-300,000 inhabitants the greatest city of the Roman east, fell to Shapur I during his second campaign, most probably in 253 (some scholars date it 256 or posit two captures). Ammianus Marcellinus, himself an Antiochene, preserves a story that the city was taken by surprise while the people sat in the theatre: an actor and his wife were performing a scene when she cried, 'Is it a dream or are the Persians here?', and the audience turned to see archers on the hill above. The Thirteenth Sibylline Oracle and later chroniclers (Malalas, Syncellus) name a renegade, Mariades or Cyriades, a member of the city council expelled for embezzlement, who led the Persians to his native city; the Historia Augusta turns him into a usurper. Shapur reportedly had him executed afterwards.

The Persians plundered the city and deported a large part of the population, including craftsmen and the bishop Demetrianus, to Persia. Shapur resettled them in new foundations such as Veh-Andiyok-Shabuhr ('Shapur's better Antioch', Gundeshapur) in Khuzestan and Bishapur in Fars, where Roman prisoners worked on buildings and mosaics; their descendants contributed to the textile, engineering and medical traditions of Sasanian Iran and formed the nucleus of the Christian church in Persia, with Greek-speaking and Syriac-speaking communities.

The sack demonstrated that the Roman east lay open. Uranius Antoninus defended Emesa and struck his own coins; Valerian, proclaimed later in 253, came east and restored Antioch's mint and defences, but Dura-Europos fell in 256 and Valerian himself was captured in 260. Antioch recovered quickly enough to become a Tetrarchic residence under Diocletian.
set.debate: Date 253 or 256; possibility of two captures.

scholarship: Downey, A History of Antioch in Syria (1961)
Potter, Prophecy and History in the Crisis of the Roman Empire (1990)

set.detail:
Dura-Europos, founded by the Seleucids on a cliff above the Euphrates and Roman since 165, was in the 250s a frontier fortress garrisoned by cohors XX Palmyrenorum and legionary vexillations, with a mixed population of Greeks, Semites, Iranians, Jews and Christians. Anticipating the Persian attack, the defenders built huge embankments of earth and mud brick against the inside of the western desert wall and filled the street behind it, burying houses including the synagogue, the Christian house church and the Mithraeum, which is why their paintings survive.

Shapur's army besieged the city around 256 (some argue 257). The Persians built a siege ramp at the south-west corner and dug mines under the wall at Tower 19 and the Palmyrene Gate. The Romans countermined, and in the tunnel under Tower 19 excavators in the 1930s found the bodies of some 19-20 Roman soldiers in arms and mail, together with one Persian. Simon James has argued (2011) that the Persians, hearing the Roman countermine approach, set a fire of bitumen and sulphur crystals and pumped the toxic smoke into the Roman gallery, killing the defenders in minutes before collapsing the tunnel with the Persian soldier caught inside: perhaps the earliest archaeological evidence of chemical warfare. The city fell, its inhabitants were killed or deported, and it was never reoccupied; Ammianus' army passed its empty ruins in 363.

Excavated by Yale and the French Academy in 1928-1937 (Cumont, Rostovtzeff), Dura became one of the most important sites in the ancient world, yielding papyri and parchments including the military records of the cohort, painted shields, horse armour, the synagogue and church paintings and the 'Pompeii of the desert'. During the Syrian civil war after 2011 the site was extensively looted, satellite images showing thousands of pits.

scholarship: James, "Stratagems, Combat, and 'Chemical Warfare' in the Siege Mines of Dura-Europos", AJA 115 (2011)
Baird, Dura-Europos (2018)

set.detail:
In 259-260, during Shapur I's third campaign, the Persians besieged Edessa and Carrhae in Osroene. Valerian, about seventy and ruling the east while his son Gallienus held the west, marched to relieve them with an army weakened by plague. What happened next is told differently by the two sides. Shapur's inscription (ŠKZ) says: 'Valerian Caesar came against us with 70,000 men from Germania, Raetia, Noricum, Dacia, Pannonia, Moesia, Istria, Spain, Africa, Thrace, Bithynia, Asia, Pamphylia, Isauria, Lycaonia, Galatia, Lycia, Cilicia, Cappadocia, Phrygia, Syria, Phoenicia, Judaea, Arabia, Mauretania, Germania, Lydia, Asia and Mesopotamia. Beyond Carrhae and Edessa a great battle took place, and we captured Valerian Caesar with our own hands, and the others, the praetorian prefect, senators and officers, all these we made prisoner and deported to Persis.' Zosimus and Zonaras instead say that Valerian, unable to break through, went to negotiate with Shapur in person with a small escort and was seized by treachery.

Valerian is the only Roman emperor ever captured by a foreign enemy. Shapur commemorated the event in rock reliefs at Naqsh-e Rostam, Bishapur and Darabgird, showing the kneeling Philip and Valerian held by the wrist. Christian writers relished his fate: Lactantius says Shapur used him as a mounting block and after his death had him flayed, his skin dyed red and hung in a temple. Roman captives were settled in Khuzestan and Fars, and a persistent tradition credits them with building the bridge-dam of Band-e Kaisar at Shushtar.

The consequences were dramatic. Gallienus did not ransom his father; the eastern army proclaimed the Macriani, Odaenathus of Palmyra emerged as Rome's champion, Postumus founded the Gallic Empire and Gallienus revoked the persecution of Christians. The battle's exact site and date (spring or summer 260; some argue 259) are uncertain.
set.debate: Battle or treacherous capture during negotiations; date 260 or 259.

scholarship: Dodgeon and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars (1991)
Canepa, The Two Eyes of the Earth (2009)

set.detail:
When news of Valerian's capture arrived, Gallienus was on the Danube facing Ingenuus and Regalianus, leaving his young son Saloninus at Colonia Agrippina under the guardianship of the praetorian prefect Silvanus, with Marcus Cassianius Latinius Postumus, a Batavian or Gallic general, in command of the Rhine. When Postumus' troops, after defeating a band of raiders, divided the booty among themselves, Silvanus demanded it be handed over. The soldiers proclaimed Postumus emperor and besieged Cologne; the citizens surrendered Saloninus, who had hastily been made Augustus, and Silvanus, and both were killed.

Postumus' regime, the Imperium Galliarum, controlled the German and Gallic provinces, Britain, Spain and, briefly, Raetia: the Augsburg victory altar, found in 1992, records a victory on 24-25 April 260 over the Semnones or Juthungi by the governor Simplicinius Genialis, dated by the consuls Postumus and Honoratianus. Its capitals were Cologne and later Trier. Postumus had a senate, consuls, a praetorian guard and good-quality coinage with types of Hercules Deusoniensis and Magusanus, and his gold is among the finest of the century. Crucially, he never tried to take Rome, presenting himself as defender of the Rhine against the Franks and Alamanni. Gallienus' campaigns against him around 265 failed, and Gallienus was wounded by an arrow.

In 269 Postumus suppressed the usurper Laelianus at Mogontiacum but refused to let his men sack the city, and they killed him. His successors Marius, Victorinus and the Tetrici lasted until Aurelian's victory at Châlons in 274. John Drinkwater's study argues that the Gallic Empire was not separatist but a Roman regime meeting regional needs that the central government could not, a view now widely accepted; the episode nonetheless foreshadowed the later regional emperors of the west.

scholarship: Drinkwater, The Gallic Empire (1987)
Bakker, "Raetien unter Postumus", Germania 71 (1993)
